hangnest: 1. A nest that hangs like a bag or pocket. 2. A bird which builds such a nest; a hangbird.
hastener: 1. One who hastens. 2. That which hastens; especially, a stand or reflector used for confining the heat of the fire to meat while roasting before it.

hagiographal: , Pertaining to the hagiographa, or to sacred writings.

hatting: The business of making hats; also, stuff for hats.
hangbird: The Baltimore oriole (Icterus galbula); -- so called because its nest is suspended from the limb of a tree. See Baltimore oriole.

hardiment: Hardihood; boldness; courage; energetic action. (old) Changing hardiment with great Glendower. Shak.

harmotome: A hydrous silicate of alumina and baryta, occurring usually in white cruciform crystals; cross-stone. Note: A related mineral, called lime harmotome, and Phillipsite, contains lime in place of baryta. Dana.
hazardize: A hazardous attempt or situation; hazard. (old) Herself had run into that hazardize. Spenser.
hatchway: A square or oblong opening in a deck or floor, affording passage from one deck or story to another; the entrance to a cellar.
hangby: A dependent; a hanger-on; -- so called in contempt. B. Jonson.
halfclammed: Half-filled. (old) Lions' half-clammed entrails roar food. Marston.
hamate: Hooked; bent at the end into a hook; hamous.
handcuff: A fastening, consisting of an iron ring around the wrist, usually connected by a chain with one on the other wrist; a manacle; -- usually in the plural. | To apply handcuffs to; to manacle. Hay (1754).
haze: Light vapor or smoke in the air which more or less impedes vision, with little or no dampness; a lack of transparency in the air; hence, figuratively, obscurity; dimness. | To be hazy, or tick with haze. Ray.
hacker: One who, or that which, hacks. Specifically: A cutting instrument for making notches; esp., one used for notching pine trees in collecting turpentine; a hack.
hall: 1. A building or room of considerable size and stateliness, used for public purposes; as, Westminster Hall, in London. 2. habituate: 1. To make accustomed; to accustom; to familiarize. Our English dogs, who were habituated to a colder clime. Sir K. Digby. Men are first corrupted . . . and next they habituate themselves to their… | Firmly established by custom; formed by habit; habitual. Hammond.
haybird: (a) The European spotted flycatcher. (b) The European blackcap.
halfcaste: One born of a European parent on the one side, and of a Hindoo or Mohammedan on the other. Also adjective; as, half-caste parents.
haughtiness: The quality of being haughty; disdain; arrogance. Syn. -- Arrogance; disdain; contemptuousness; superciliousness; loftiness. -- Haughtiness, Arrogance, Disdain. handbook: A book of reference, to be carried in the hand; a manual; a guidebook.
habitue: One who habitually frequents a place; as, an habitué of a theater.
halcyon: A kingfisher. By modern ornithologists restricted to a genus including a limited number of species having omnivorous habits, as the sacred kingfisher (Halcyon sancta) of Australia. | 1. haliotis: A genus of marine shells; the ear-shells. See Abalone.
hatchboat: A vessel whose deck consists almost wholly of movable hatches; -- used mostly in the fisheries.
haslet: The edible viscera, as the heart, liver, etc., of a beast, esp. of a hog. [Written also harslet.]
hatchetman: 1. A person hired to murder or physically attack another; a hit man. 2. A person who deliberately tries to ruin the reputation of another, often unscrupulously, by slander or other malicious communication, often with political motive, and sometimes for pay.
haemad: Toward the hæmal side; on the hæmal side of; -- opposed to neurad.
haunted: Inhabited by, or subject to the visits of, apparitions; frequented by a ghost. All houses wherein men have lived and died Are haunted houses. Longfellow.
harmless: 1. Free from harm; unhurt; as, to give bond to save another harmless. 2. Free from power or disposition to harm; innocent; inoffensive. " The harmless deer." haver: The oat; oats. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Haver bread, oaten bread. -- Haver cake, oaten cake. Piers Plowman. -- Haver grass, the wild oat. -- Haver meal, oatmeal. | To maunder; to talk foolishly; to chatter. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.
hagridden: Ridden by a hag or witch; hence, afflicted with nightmare. Beattie. Cheyne.
harderian: A term applied to a lachrymal gland on the inner side of the orbit of many animals which have a third eyelid, or nictitating membrane. See Nictitating membrane, under Nictitate.
haidingerite: A mineral consisting of the arseniate of lime; -- so named in honor of W. Haidinger, of Vienna.
hardfisted: 1. Having hard or strong hands; as, a hard-fisted laborer. 2. Close-fisted; covetous; niggardly. Bp. Hall.
hatter: To tire or worry; -- out. (old) Dryden.
hardheaded: Having sound judgment; sagacious; shrewd. -- Hard"-head`ed*ness, n.
harem: 1. The apartments or portion of the house allotted to females in Mohammedan families. 2. The family of wives and concubines belonging to one man, in Mohammedan countries; a seraglio.
hanoverian: Of or pertaining to Hanover or its people, or to the House of Hanover in England. | A native or naturalized inhabitant of Hanover; one of the House of Hanover.
hare: To excite; to tease, or worry; to harry. (old) Locke. | 1. (Zoöl.) A rodent of the genus Lepus, having long hind legs, a short tail, and a divided upper lip. It is a timid animal, moves swiftly by leaps, and is remarkable for its fecundity.
hairspring: The slender recoil spring which regulates the motion of the balance in a timepiece.
handwriting: 1. The cast or form of writing peculiar to each hand or person; chirography. 2. That which is written by hand; manuscript. The handwriting on the wall, a doom pronounced; an omen of disaster. Dan. v. 5.
happed: Wrapped; covered; cloaked. [Scot.] All happed with flowers in the green wood were. Hogg.
haplomi: An order of freshwater fishes, including the true pikes, cyprinodonts, and blindfishes.
hark: To listen; to hearken. [Now rare, except in the imperative form used as an interjection, Hark! listen.] Hudibras. Hark away! Hark back! Hark forward! (Sporting), cries used to incite and guide hounds in hunting. -- To hark back, to go back for a fresh start, as when one has wandered from his direct course, or made a digression.
hardfavored: Hard-featured; ill-looking; as, Vulcan was hard-favored. Dryden.
haul: 1. To pull or draw with force; to drag. Some dance, some haul the rope. Denham. Thither they bent, and hauled their ships to land. Pope. Romp-loving miss Is hauled about in gallantry robust. haircloth: Stuff or cloth made wholly or in part of hair.
harmonious: 1. Adapted to each other; having parts proportioned to each other; symmetrical. God hath made the intellectual world harmonious and beautiful without us. Locke. 2. Acting together to a common end; agreeing in action or feeling; living in peace and friendship; as, an harmonious family. 3. Vocally or musically concordant; agreeably consonant; symphonious.
hattisherif: A irrevocable Turkish decree countersigned by the sultan.
hazardry: 1. Playing at hazard; gaming; gambling. Chaucer. 2. Rashness; temerity. Spenser.
handle: 1. To touch; to feel with the hand; to use or hold with the hand. Handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh. Luke xxiv. 39. About his altar, handling holy things. Milton. 2. | To use the hands. They have hands, but they handle not. Ps. cxv. 7.
hammercloth: The cloth which covers a coach box.
hallux: The first, or preaxial, digit of the hind limb, corresponding to the pollux in the fore limb; the great toe; the hind toe of birds.
hardhearted: Unsympathetic; inexorable; cruel; pitiless. -- Hard"-heart`ed*ness, n.
hareld: The long-tailed duck. See Old Squaw.
harquebuse: A firearm with match holder, trigger, and tumbler, made in the second half of the 15th century. the barrel was about forty inches long. A form of the harquebus was subsequently called arquebus with matchlock.
halma: The long jump, with weights in the hands, -- the most important of the exercises of the Pentathlon.
hatch: 1. To cross with lines in a peculiar manneHatching. Shall win this sword, silvered and hatched. Chapman. Those hatching strokes of the pencil. Dryden. 2. hat: sing. pres. of Hote to be called. Cf. Hatte. (old) "That one hat abstinence." Piers Plowman. | A covering for the head; esp., one with a crown and brim, made of various materials, and worn by men or women for protecting the head from the sun or weather, or for ornament.
hackmatack: The American larch (Larix Americana), a coniferous tree with slender deciduous leaves; also, its heavy, close-grained timber. Called also tamarack.

haruspice: A diviner of ancient Rome. Same as Aruspice.
hardlabored: Wrought with severe labor; elaborate; studied. Swift.
hawkeyed: Having a keen eye; sharpsighted; discerning.
hautein: 1. Haughty; proud. (old) Chaucer. 2. High; -- said of the voice or flight of birds. (old)
halfness: The quality of being half; incompleteness. As soon as there is any departure from simplicity, and attempt at halfness, or good for me that is not good for him, my neighbor feels the wrong. Emerson.
haemal: Pertaining to the blood or blood vessels; also, ventral. See Hemal.
halved: Appearing as if one side, or one half, were cut away; dimidiate.
hask: A basket made of rushes or flags, as for carrying fish. (old) Spenser.
hartwort: A coarse umbelliferous plant of Europe (Tordylium maximum). Note: The name is often vaguely given to other plants of the same order, as species of Seseli and Bupleurum.
hance: To raise; to elevate. (old) Lydgate. | 1. (Arch.) See Hanse. 2. (Naut.) A sudden fall or break, as the fall of the fife rail down to the gangway.
hairy: Bearing or covered with hair; made of or resembling hair; rough with hair; rough with hair; rough with hair; hirsute. His mantle hairy, and his bonnet sedge. Milton.
hackee: The chipmunk; also, the chickaree or red squirrel. [U.S.]
halotrichite: An iron alum occurring in silky fibrous aggregates of a yellowish white color.
haloscope: An instrument for exhibition or illustration of the phenomena of halos, parhelia, and the like.
hamper: A large basket, usually with a cover, used for the packing and carrying of articles; as, a hamper of wine; a clothes hamper; an oyster hamper, which contains two bushels. | To put a hamper or fetter on; to shackle; to insnare; to inveigle; hence, to impede in motion or progress; to embarrass; to encumber. hauteur: Haughty manner or spirit; haughtiness; pride; arrogance.

hamulus: 1. (Anat.) A hook, or hooklike process. 2. (Zoöl.) A hooked barbicel of a feather.
hawfinch: The common European grosbeak (Coccothraustes vulgaris); -- called also cherry finch, and coble.
haymaker: 1. One who cuts and cures hay. 2. A machine for curing hay in rainy weather.
halfheard: Imperfectly or partly heard to the end. And leave half-heard the melancholy tale. Pope.
haloxyline: An explosive mixture, consisting of sawdust, charcoal, niter, and ferrocyanide of potassium, used as a substitute for gunpowder.
haplostemonous: Having but one series of stamens, and that equal in number to the proper number of petals; isostemonous.
harakiri: Suicide, by slashing the abdomen, formerly practiced in Japan, and commanded by the government in the cases of disgraced officials; disembowelment; -- also written, but incorrectly, hari-kari. W. E. Griffis.
halfread: Informed by insufficient reading; superficial; shallow. Dryden.
hart: A stag; the male of the red deer. See the Note under Buck. Goodliest of all the forest, hart and hind. Milton.
harmost: A governor or prefect appointed by the Spartans in the cities subjugated by them.
hamburg: A commercial city of Germany, near the mouth of the Elbe. Black Hamburg grape. See under Black. -- Hamburg , a kind of embroidered work done by machinery on cambric or muslin; -- used for trimming. -- Hamburg lake, a purplish crimson pigment resembling cochineal.
hammerharden: To harden, as a metal, by hammering it in the cold state.

harpress: A female harper. Sir W. Scott.
harmonicon: A small, flat, wind instrument of music, in which the notes are produced by the vibration of free metallic reeds.
haematoplastic: Blood formative; -- applied to a substance in early fetal life, which breaks up gradually into blood vessels.

harmful: Full of harm; injurious; hurtful; mischievous. " Most harmful hazards." Strype. --Harm"ful*ly, adv. -- Harm"ful*ness, n.

haiduck: Formerly, a mercenary foot soldier in Hungary, now, a halberdier of a Hungarian noble, or an attendant in German or Hungarian courts. [Written also hayduck, heiduc, heiduck, and heyduk.]

harping: Pertaining to the harp; as, harping symphonies. Milton.

halfhearted: 1. Wanting in heart or spirit; ungenerous; unkind. B. Jonson. 2. Lacking zeal or courage; lukewarm. H. James.

handwheel: Any wheel worked by hand; esp., one the rim of which serves as the handle by which a valve, car brake, or other part is adjusted.
hault: Lofty; haughty. (old) Through support of countenance proud and hault. Spenser.
haven: 1. A bay, recess, or inlet of the sea, or the mouth of a river, which affords anchorage and shelter for shipping; a harbor; a port. What shipping and what lading's in our haven. Shak. | To shelter, as in a haven. Keats.
haematitic: Of a blood-red color; crimson; (Bot.) brownish red.
hamitic: Pertaining to Ham or his descendants. Hamitic languages, the group of languages spoken mainly in the Sahara, Egypt, Galla, and Somâli Land, and supposed to be allied to the Semitic. Keith Johnson.
hallier: A kind of net for catching birds.
hamous: Having the end hooked or curved.
hartshorn: 1. The horn or antler of the hart, or male red deer. 2. Spirits of hartshorn (see below); volatile salts. halfpike: A short pike, sometimes carried by officers of infantry, sometimes used in boarding ships; a spontoon. Tatler.
hatchment: 1. (Her.) A sort of panel, upon which the arms of a deceased person are temporarily displayed, -- usually on the walls of his dwelling. hater: One who hates. An enemy to God, and a hater of all good. Sir T. Browne.

hawkbill: A sea turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata), which yields the best quality of tortoise shell; -- called also caret.
hachure: A short line used in drawing and engraving, especially in shading and denoting different surfaces, as in map drawing. See Hatching.
hailstorm: A storm accompanied with hail; a shower of hail.
hagiographa: 1. The last of the three Jewish divisions of the Old Testament, or that portion not contained in the Law and the Prophets. hawker: One who sells wares by crying them in the street; hence, a peddler or a packman. | To sell goods by outcry in the street. (old) Hudibras.
hardsteel: Steel hardened by the addition of other elements, as manganese, phosphorus, or (usually) carbon.
harass: To fatigue; to tire with repeated and exhausting efforts; esp., to weary by importunity, teasing, or fretting; to cause to endure excessive burdens or anxieties; -- sometimes followed by out. | 1. Devastation; waste. (old) Milton. 2. Worry; harassment. Byron.
hammer: 1. An instrument for driving nails, beating metals, and the like, consisting of a head, usually of steel or iron, fixed crosswise to a handle. With busy hammers closing rivets up. Shak. 2. | 1. To beat with a hammer; to beat with heavy blows; as, to hammer iron. 2. To form or forge with a hammer; to shape by beating. "Hammered money." Dryden. 3. To form in the mind;
handbreadth: A space equal to the breadth of the hand; a palm. Ex. xxxvii. 12.
haematoin: A substance formed from the hematin of blood, by removal of the iron through the action of concentrated sulphuric acid. Two like bodies, called respectively hæmatoporphyrin and hæmatolin, are formed in a similar manner.
handfast: 1. Hold; grasp; custody; power of confining or keeping. (old) Shak. 2. Contract; specifically, espousal. (old) | Fast by contract; betrothed by joining hands. (old) Bale.
halfandhalf: A mixture of two malt liquors, esp. porter and ale, in about equal parts. Dickens.
hamstring: One of the great tendons situated in each side of the ham, or space back of the knee, and connected with the muscles of the back of the thigh. | To lame or disable by cutting the tendons of the ham or knee; to hough; hence, to cripple; to incapacitate; to disable. So have they hamstrung the valor of the subject by seeking to effeminate us all…
hackster: A bully; a bravo; a ruffian; an assassin. (old) Milton.
handsaw: A saw used with one hand.
harmonic: 1. Concordant; musical; consonant; as, harmonic sounds. Harmonic twang! of leather, horn, and brass. Pope. 2. (Mus.) Relating to harmony, -- as melodic relates to melody; harmonious; | A musical note produced by a number of vibrations which is a multiple of the number producing some other; an overtone. See Harmonics.
hamulate: Furnished with a small hook; hook-shaped. Gray.
harmonium: A musical instrument, resembling a small organ and especially designed for church music, in which the tones are produced by forcing air by means of a bellows so as to cause the vibration of free metallic reeds. It is now made with one or two keyboards, and has pedals and stops.
hastated: Shaped like the head of a halberd; triangular, with the basal angles or lobes spreading; as, a hastate leaf.
hades: The nether world (according to classical mythology, the abode of the shades, ruled over by Hades or Pluto); the invisible world; the grave. And death and Hades gave up the dead which were in them. Rev. xx. 13 (Rev. Ver. ). Neither was he left in Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. Acts ii. 31 (Rev. Ver.). And in Hades he lifted up his eyes, being in torments.
haematolysis: Dissolution of the red blood corpuscles with diminished coagulability of the blood; hæmolysis. -- Hæm`a*to*lyt"ic (#), a.
harbinger: 1. One who provides lodgings; especially, the officer of the English royal household who formerly preceded the court when traveling, to provide and prepare lodgings. Fuller. 2. A forerunner; | To usher in; to be a harbinger of. "Thus did the star of religious freedom harbinger the day." Bancroft.
handsel: 1. A sale, gift, or delivery into the hand of another; especially, a sale, gift, delivery, or using which is the first of a series, and regarded as on omen for the rest; a first installment; | 1. To give a handsel to. 2. To use or do for the first time, esp. so as to make fortunate or unfortunate; to try experimentally. No contrivance of our body, but some good man in Scripture hath…
hairsalt: A variety of native Epsom salt occurring in silky fibers.
hamular: Hooked; hooklike; hamate; as, the hamular process of the sphenoid bone.
haggis: A Scotch pudding made of the heart, liver, lights, etc., of a sheep or lamb, minced with suet, onions, oatmeal, etc., highly seasoned, and boiled in the stomach of the same animal; minced head and pluck. [Written also haggiss, haggess, and haggies.]
hardfern: A species of fern (Lomaria borealis), growing in Europe and Northwestern America.
habendum: That part of a deed which follows the part called the premises, and determines the extent of the interest or estate granted; -- so called because it begins with the word Habendum. Kent.
harshly: In a harsh manner; gratingly; roughly; rudely. 'T will sound harshly in her ears. Shak.
hamamelis: A genus of plants which includes the witch-hazel (Hamamelis Virginica), a preparation of which is used medicinally.
hatte: pres. & imp. sing. & pl. of Hote, to be called. See Hote. (old) Chaucer. A full perilous place, purgatory it hatte. Piers Plowman.
hallucinatory: Partaking of, or tending to produce, hallucination.
habitus: Habitude; mode of life; general appearance.
halimas: The feast of All Saints; Hallowmas. (old)
harbormaster: An officer charged with the duty of executing the regulations respecting the use of a harbor.
halwe: A saint. (old) Chaucer. HAL'YARD; HALYARD Hal'yard, n. Etym: [Hale, v. t. + yard.] (Naut.) A rope or tackle for hoisting or lowering yards, sails, flags, etc. [Written also halliard, haulyard.]
haggler: 1. One who haggles or is difficult in bargaining. 2. One who forestalls a market; a middleman between producer and dealer in London vegetable markets.
halloo: A loud exclamation; a call to invite attention or to incite a person or an animal; a shout. List! List! I hear Some far off halloo break the silent air. Milton. | To cry out; to exclaim with a loud voice; to call to a person, as by the word halloo. Country folks hallooed and hooted after me. Sir P. Sidney.
handwinged: Having wings that are like hands in the structure and arrangement of their bones; -- said of bats. See Cheiroptera.
hastypudding: 1. A thick batter pudding made of Indian meal stirred into boiling water; mush. [U. S.] 2. A batter or pudding made of flour or oatmeal, stirred into boiling water or milk. [Eng.]
hanging: 1. Requiring, deserving, or foreboding death by the halter. "What a hanging face!" Dryden. 2. Suspended from above; pendent; as, hanging shelves. 3. Adapted for sustaining a hanging object; | 1. The act of suspending anything; the state of being suspended. 2. Death by suspension; execution by a halter. 3. That which is hung as lining or drapery for the walls of a room, as tapestry, paper,…
haemony: A plant described by Milton as "of sovereign use against all enchantments."
handling: 1. A touching, controlling, managing, using, etc., with the hand or hands, or as with the hands. See Handle, v. t. The heavens and your fair handling Have made you master of the field this day. Spenser. 2. (Drawing, Painting, etc.) The mode of using the pencil or brush, etc.; style of touch. Fairholt.
hazard: 1. A game of chance played with dice. Chaucer. 2. The uncertain result of throwing a die; hence, a fortuitous event; chance; accident; casualty. I will stand the hazard of the die. Shak. 3. Risk; | 1. To expose to the operation of chance; to put in danger of loss or injury; to venture; to risk. Men hazard nothing by a course of evangelical obedience. John Clarke.
halysites: A genus of Silurian fossil corals; the chain corals. See Chain coral, under Chain.
haycutter: A machine in which hay is chopped short, as fodder for cattle.
hanukka: The Jewish Feast of the Dedication, instituted by Judas Maccabæus, his brothers, and the whole congregation of Israel, in 165 b. c., to commemorate the dedication of the new altar set up at the purification of the temple of Jerusalem to replace the altar which had been polluted by Antiochus Epiphanes (1 Maccabees i. 58, iv. 59). The feast, which is mentioned in John x.
harpist: A player on the harp; a harper. W. Browne.
halacha: The general term for the Hebrew oral or traditional law; one of two branches of exposition in the Midrash. See Midrash.
halfmast: A point some distance below the top of a mast or staff; as, a flag a half-mast (a token of mourning, etc.).
hankeypankey: Professional cant; the chatter of conjurers to divert attention from their tricks; hence, jugglery. [Colloq.]
haematology: The science which treats of the blood. Same as Hematology.
harry: 1. To strip; to lay waste; as, the Northmen came several times and harried the land. To harry this beautiful region. W. Irving. A red squirrel had harried the nest of a wood thrush. J. Burroughs. 2. | To make a predatory incursion; to plunder or lay waste. (old) Beau. & Fl.
hagberry: A plant of the genus Prunus (P. Padus); the bird cherry. [Scot.]
halfboot: A boot with a short top covering only the ankle. See Cocker, and Congress boot, under Congress.
hamulose: Bearing a small hook at the end. Gray.
hairbrush: A brush for cleansing and smoothing the hair.
harpsichord: A harp-shaped instrument of music set horizontally on legs, like the grand piano, with strings of wire, played by the fingers, by means of keys provided with quills, instead of hammers, for striking the strings. It is now superseded by the piano.
harlock: Probably a corruption either of charlock or hardock. Drayton.
hagborn: Born of a hag or witch. Shak.
habitual: 1. Formed or acquired by habit or use. An habitual knowledge of certain rules and maxims. South. 2. According to habit; established by habit; customary; constant; as, the habiual practice of sin. It is the distinguishing mark of habitual piety to be grateful for the most common and ordinary blessings. Buckminster. Syn. -- Customary; accustomed; usual; common; wonted; ordinary;
hallucinator: One whose judgment and acts are affected by hallucinations; one who errs on account of his hallucinations. N. Brit. Rev.
haema: Combining forms indicating relation or resemblance to blood, association with blood; as, hæmapod, hæmatogenesis, hæmoscope. Note: Words from Gr. (hema-, hemato-, hemo-, as well as hæma-, hæmato-, hæmo-.
harelip: A lip, commonly the upper one, having a fissure of perpendicular division like that of a hare. -- Hare"lipped`, a.
haversack: 1. A bag for oats or oatmeal. [Prov. Eng.] 2. A bag or case, usually of stout cloth, in which a soldier carries his rations when on a march; -- distinguished from knapsack. 3. A gunner's case or bag used carry cartridges from the ammunition chest to the piece in loading.
harvest: 1. The gathering of a crop of any kind; the ingathering of the crops; also, the season of gathering grain and fruits, late summer or early autumn. Seedtime and harvest . . . shall not cease. | To reap or gather, as any crop.
haberdashery: The goods and wares sold by a haberdasher; also (Fig.), trifles. Burke.
harvestry: The act of harvesting; also, that which is harvested. Swinburne.
hastily: 1. In haste; with speed or quickness; speedily; nimbly. 2. Without due reflection; precipitately; rashly. We hastily engaged in the war. Swift. 3. Passionately; impatiently. Shak.
halfport: One half of a shutter made in two parts for closing a porthole.
harvestman: 1. A man engaged in harvesting. Shak. 2. (Zoöl.) See Daddy longlegs, 1.
harmony: 1. The just adaptation of parts to each other, in any system or combination of things, or in things, or things intended to form a connected whole; such an agreement between the different parts of a design or composition as to produce unity of effect; as, the harmony of the universe. 2. Concord or agreement in facts, opinions, manners, interests, etc.; good correspondence;
haulabout: A bargelike vessel with steel hull, large hatchways, and coal transporters, for coaling war vessels from its own hold or from other colliers.
having: Possession; goods; estate. I 'll lend you something; my having is not much. Shak.
hartford: The Hartford grape, a variety of grape first raised at Hartford, Connecticut, from the Northern fox grape. Its large dark- colored berries ripen earlier than those of most other kinds. HART'S CLOVER Hart's` clo`ver. (Bot.) Melilot or sweet clover. See Melilot. HART'S-EAR Hart's`-ear`, n. (Bot.) An Asiatic species of Cacalia (C. Kleinia), used medicinally in India.
hatchel: An instrument with long iron teeth set in a board, for cleansing flax or hemp from the tow, hards, or coarse part; a kind of large comb; -- called also hackle and heckle. | 1. To draw through the teeth of a hatchel, as flax or hemp, so as to separate the coarse and refuse parts from the fine, fibrous parts. 2. To tease; to worry; to torment. [Colloq.]
haemoscope: An instrument devised by Hermann, for regulating and measuring the thickness of a layer of blood for spectroscopic examination.
harlequinade: A play or part of play in which the harlequin is conspicuous; the part of a harlequin. Macaulay.
hayfork: A fork for pitching and tedding hay. Horse hayfork, a contrivance for unloading hay from the cart and depositing it in the loft, or on a mow, by horse power.
hardvisaged: Of a harsh or stern countenance; hard-featured. Burke.
harlot: 1. A churl; a common man; a person, male or female, of low birth. (old) He was a gentle harlot and a kind. Chaucer. 2. A person given to low conduct; a rogue; a cheat; a rascal. (old) Chaucer. 3. | Wanton; lewd; low; base. Shak.
hairsplitter: One who makes excessively nice or needless distinctions in reasoning; one who quibbles. "The caviling hairsplitter." De Quincey.
haematosac: A vascular sac connected, beneath the brain, in many fishes, with the infundibulum.
hardly: 1. In a hard or difficult manner; with difficulty. Recovering hardly what he lost before. Dryden. 2. Unwillingly; grudgingly. The House of Peers gave so hardly theiMilton. 3. Scarcely; barely; not guite; not wholly. Hardly shall you one so bad, but he desires the credit of being thought good. South. 4. Severely; harshly; roughly. He has in many things been hardly used. Swift.
haltingly: In a halting or limping manner.
halituous: Produced by, or like, breath; vaporous. Boyle.
hay: 1. A hedge. (old) 2. A net set around the haunt of an animal, especially of a rabbit. Rowe. To dance the hay, to dance in a ring. Shak. | To lay snares for rabbits. Huloet.
habergeon: Properly, a short hauberk, but often used loosely for the hauberk. Chaucer.
handicraftsman: A man skilled or employed in handcraft. Bacon.
handtight: As tight as can be made by the hand. Totten.
hastate: Shaped like the head of a halberd; triangular, with the basal angles or lobes spreading; as, a hastate leaf.
hapuku: A large and valuable food fish (Polyprion prognathus) of New Zealand. It sometimes weighs one hundred pounds or more.
haemochromometer: An apparatus for measuring the amount of hemoglobin in a fluid, by comparing it with a solution of known strength and of normal color.
haustellate: Provided with a haustellum, or sucking proboscis. -- n. One of the Haustellata.
hackery: A cart with wooden wheels, drawn by bullocks. [Bengal] Malcom.
hagbut: A harquebus, of which the but was bent down or hooked for convenience in taking aim. [Written also haguebut and hackbuss.]
habeascorpus: A writ having for its object to bring a party before a court or judge; especially, one to inquire into the cause of a person's imprisonment or detention by another, with the view to protect the right to personal liberty; also, one to bring a prisoner into court to testify in a pending trial. Bouvier.
hairen: Hairy. [Obc.] His hairen shirt and his ascetic diet. J. Taylor.
hagiarchy: A sacred government; by holy orders of men. Southey.
harrower: One who harrows. | One who harries. (old)
haje: The Egyptian asp or cobra (Naja haje.) It is related to the cobra of India, and like the latter has the power of inflating its neck into a hood. Its bite is very venomous. It is supposed to be the snake by means of whose bite Cleopatra committed suicide, and hence is sometimes called Cleopatra's snake or asp. See Asp.
haemapoietic: Bloodforming; as, the hæmapoietic function of the spleen.
haminura: A large edible river fish (Erythrinus macrodon) of Guiana.
harridan: A worn-out strumpet; a vixenish woman; a hag. Such a weak, watery, wicked old harridan, substituted for the pretty creature I had been used to see. De Quincey.
haemacyanin: A substance found in the blood of the octopus, which gives to it its blue color. Note: When deprived of oxygen it is colorless, but becomes quickly blue in contact with oxygen, and is then generally called oxyhæmacyanin. A similar blue coloring matter has been detected in small quantity in the blood of other animals and in the bile.
halfendeal: Half; by the part. (old) Chaucer. -- n. A half part. (old) R. of Brunne.
haggle: To cut roughly or hack; to cut into small pieces; to notch or cut in an unskillful manner; to make rough or mangle by cutting; as, a boy haggles a stick of wood. Suffolk first died, and York, all… | To be difficult in bargaining; to stick at small matters; to chaffer; to higgle. Royalty and science never haggled about the value of blood. Walpole.
haematocrya: The cold-blooded vertebrates. Same as Hematocrya.
hassock: 1. A rank tuft of bog grass; a tussock. Forby. 2. A small stuffed cushion or footstool, for kneeling on in church, or for home use. And knees and hassocks are well nigh divorced. Cowper.
halt: 3d pers. sing. pres. of Hold, contraction for holdeth. (old) Chaucer. | A stop in marching or walking, or in any action; arrest of progress. Without any halt they marched. Clarendon. [Lovers] soon in passion's war contest, Yet in their march soon make a halt. Davenant.
hatching: A mode of execution in engraving, drawing, and miniature painting, in which shading is produced by lines crossing each other at angles more or less acute; -- called also crosshatching.
hate: 1. To have a great aversion to, with a strong desire that evil should befall the person toward whom the feeling is directed; to dislike intensely; to detest; as, to hate one's enemies; | Strong aversion coupled with desire that evil should befall the person toward whom the feeling is directed; as exercised toward things, intense dislike; hatred; detestation; -- opposed to love.
harebell: A small, slender, branching plant (Campanula rotundifolia), having blue bell-shaped flowers; also, Scilla nutans, which has similar flowers; -- called also bluebell. [Written also hairbell.] E'en the light harebell raised its head. Sir W. Scott .
haulage: Act of hauling; as, the haulage of cars by an engine; charge for hauling.
halogen: An electro-negative element or radical, which, by combination with a metal, forms a haloid salt; especially, chlorine, bromine, and iodine; sometimes, also, fluorine and cyanogen. See Chlorine family, under Chlorine.
halfdecked: Partially decked. The half-decked craft . . . used by the latter Vikings. Elton.
haematoxylon: A genus of leguminous plants containing but a single species, the H. Campechianum or logwood tree, native in Yucatan.
hatteria: A New Zealand lizard, which, in anatomical character, differs widely from all other existing lizards. It is the only living representative of the order Rhynchocephala, of which many Mesozoic fossil species are known; -- called also Sphenodon, and Tuatera.
haemacytometer: An apparatus for determining the number of corpuscles in a given quantity of blood.
harangue: A speech addressed to a large public assembly; a popular oration; a loud address a multitude; in a bad sense, a noisy or pompous speech; declamation; ranting. Gray-headed men and grave, with warriors… | To make an harangue; to declaim.
hatchery: A house for hatching fish, etc.
hansomcab: A light, low, two-wheeled covered carriage with the driver's seat elevated behind, the reins being passed over the top. He hailed a cruising hansom . . . " 'Tis the gondola of London," said Lothair. Beaconsfield. HAN'T; HAIN'T Han't. A contraction of have not, or has not, used in illiterate speech. In the United States the commoner spelling is hain't.
halfbeak: Any slender, marine fish of the genus Hemirhamphus, having the upper jaw much shorter than the lower; -- called also balahoo.
halfhourly: Done or happening at intervals of half an hour.
hardfeatured: Having coarse, unattractive or stern features. Smollett.
hards: The refuse or coarse part of fiax; tow.
hag: 1. A witch, sorceress, or enchantress; also, a wizard. (old) "[Silenus] that old hag." Golding. 2. An ugly old woman. 3. A fury; a she-monster. Grashaw. 4. (Zoöl.) An eel-like marine marsipobranch… | To harass; to weary with vexation. How are superstitious men hagged out of their wits with the fancy of omens. L'Estrange.
hairstreak: A butterfly of the genus Thecla; as, the green hairstreak (T. rubi).
handily: In a handy manner; skillfully; conveniently.
haemato: Combining forms indicating relation or resemblance to blood, association with blood; as, hæmapod, hæmatogenesis, hæmoscope. Note: Words from Gr. (hema-, hemato-, hemo-, as well as hæma-, hæmato-, hæmo-.
harassment: The act of harassing, or state of being harassed; worry; annoyance; anxiety. Little harassments which I am led to suspect do occasionally molest the most fortunate. Ld. Lytton.
harmaline: An alkaloid found in the plant Peganum harmala. It forms bitter, yellow salts.
hatred: Strong aversion; intense dislike; hate; an affection of the mind awakened by something regarded as evil. Syn. -- Odium; ill will; enmity; hate; animosity; malevolence; rancor; malignity; detestation; loathing; abhorrence; repugnance; antipathy. See Odium.
hardgrass: A name given to several different grasses, especially to the Roltböllia incurvata, and to the species of Ægilops, from one of which it is contended that wheat has been derived.
hardness: 1. The quality or state of being hard, literally or figuratively. The habit of authority also had given his manners some peremptory hardness. Sir W. Scott. 2. (Min.) The cohesion of the particles on the surface of a body, determined by its capacity to scratch another, or be itself scratched;-measured among minerals on a scale of which diamond and talc form the extremes. 3.
hawkmoth: Any moth of the family Sphingidæ, of which there are numerous genera and species. They are large, handsome moths, which fly mostly at twilight and hover about flowers like a humming bird, sucking the honey by means of a long, slender proboscis. The larvæ are large, hairless caterpillars ornamented with green and other bright colors, and often with a caudal spine.
